lead: Power cycles turn heat into work and refrigeration cycles spend work or heat to move heat from cold to hot. This unit models the petrol, diesel and gas-turbine engines with air standard cycles, the steam plant with the Rankine cycle and its reheat and regenerative forms, and cooling with the vapour compression and vapour absorption cycles. After it you can sketch each cycle, fix its states from gas relations or property tables, and compute its efficiency or COP, work, mean effective pressure and steam or refrigerant flow.
about: The first four chapters treat gas cycles. The air standard assumptions turn an engine into a loop of ideal air, with the Carnot cycle as the limit. The Otto, Diesel and Dual cycles model piston engines, the Brayton and Stirling cycles model the gas turbine and the external-heat engine, and the chapter on efficiency and mean effective pressure compares them on fair bases. The next two chapters move to steam, where the fluid changes phase: the Rankine cycle and the effect of pressure and temperature, then reheat and regeneration. The last two run a cycle backwards for cooling, first with a compressor and then with heat. Every chapter answers the same question with real numbers: how much work, or how much cooling, for the energy supplied.
